DaVinci Resolve + Local AI Workstation

A complete, scripted post-production workstation: Claude Code driven by a fully local LLM, operating DaVinci Resolve Studio through three MCP servers, with Blender rendered headless for titles and generated content, and a live observability dashboard — on one Apple Silicon Mac, no cloud, no API keys for the editor path.

People kept asking how the setup works; this repo is the answer, as scripts.

┌─────────────────────────────  one Mac Studio (Apple Silicon)  ─────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                                           │
│  Splash (brew) ── serves Qwen Flash-Next IQ3_S on :8000  ←→  splash-dashboard on :8280    │
│      │  OpenAI-compat + Anthropic-compat; persistent SSD prefix cache                     │
│      ▼                                                                                    │
│  Claude Code  (splash claude — the agent IS the model you run locally)                    │
│      │  MCP (stdio)                                                                       │
│      ├── davinci-resolve            community Python MCP  — live editing/render/guardrails │
│      ├── davinci-resolve-advanced   community Node MCP    — offline DB/DRX/DRT/QC          │
│      ├── DaVinci Resolve            official Blackmagic MCP (ships in Studio 21.1+)       │
│      ├── brave-search (optional)    official Brave MCP    — web research (paid key)       │
│      ▼                                                                                    │
│  DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2  ←── EXR title sequences rendered by headless Blender        │
│      ▲                                       (Cycles on Metal, film_transparent)          │
│      └── ffmpeg/ffprobe — QC read-backs, sequence encoding, frame extraction              │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What each piece brings

Tool Benefit
Splash (incoai/tap, brew) Local LLM engine serving Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S (262k context, GGUF/IQ3 quant) behind OpenAI and Anthropic-compatible APIs. Persistent disk prefix-cache means fresh agent sessions reuse ~20–45k cached tokens each. TTFT ~200 ms warm; single-stream decode ~170 tok/s; aggregate plateau ~375 tok/s under concurrency. Also hosts a built-in chat UI on :8000.
Claude Code via splash claude The agentic operator. Reads the timeline, plans edits, executes them through MCP with dry-run/confirm-token discipline, verifies via read-backs, renders, grades its own output with ffprobe. Nothing leaves the machine.
Community davinci-resolve MCP (samuelgursky/davinci-resolve-mcp) The hands: ~36 action-dispatch tools over the whole scripting API — media pool, timelines, ripple edits with dry-run plans, markers, Fusion comps, render queue + verified outputs (ffprobe cross-check of every render), and a live api_truth knowledge base of verified Resolve API quirks. Destructive ops auto-archive timelines first.
davinci-resolve-advanced MCP (same project) The forensic layer: closed-Project.db reads/writes (captions, speed ramps), .drx grade XML, DRT timelines, FCPXML/EDL/AAF conform, deliverable-QC specs — all without Resolve running.
Official ResolveMCP (bundled in Resolve Studio 21.1+) Blackmagic's own 18-tool surface: canonical and versioned with the app; useful cross-check and fallback.
Brave Search MCP (opt-in: official @brave/brave-search-mcp-server, MIT) The research leg — the only one that costs money: live fact-checks no model can know, like whether a new Resolve build changed an API behaviour or whether an upstream release has wheels on PyPI yet. Priced $5 per 1,000 queries, with $5 of free credit applied automatically every month (~1,000 free queries; card required at signup even for free use). The only leg where queries leave the machine — search strings get the same scrubbing discipline as commit messages. Setup, pricing details and a plan-bound-key gotcha in mcp/mcp-config.md.
splash-dashboard (rickhuizinga/splash-dashboard) Live engine observability on :8280: KV residency, prefix-cache hit rate, admission pacing, decode batch widths — the instrument panel that turns "the model feels slow" into numbers.
Prometheus + Grafana (opt-in; --no-metrics to skip) History leg: the engine serves native Prometheus text at /metrics (~130 splash_* series), Prometheus scrapes it at 15 s, and a provisioned Grafana dashboard (:3000) graphs scheduler/admission states, decode batch-width mix, KV pages, SSD-cache IO and TTFT/ITL quantiles with 15 days of retention. Provisioning is file-based, so a fresh machine reproduces it; the one gotcha: Grafana 13 renamed its provisioning ini keys — [paths] provisioning = … plus permitted_provisioning_paths, or provisioning silently loads nothing.
Blender (LTS, at /Applications) Content forge: 3D title stings, extruded logos, generated media — scripted headless (--background --python), rendered transparent-EXR, imported into Resolve as sequence clips with straight alpha. See blender/.
ffmpeg / ffprobe (brew) The verification layer: every render gets probed (frame count, codecs, duration) before it's trusted; sequence encoding; frame extraction for visual checks.
whisper.cpp / whisper CLI (brew + MCP-integrated) Local transcription; the MCP server also feeds transcripts into timeline subtitle tracks and cut-candidate proposals.
Vision add-on (opt-in: install.sh --vision, see vision/) Face-level signals off Resolve: OpenCV YuNet + SFace for detection/identity and MediaPipe for landmarks, in their own Python 3.12 venv. 90 faces detected on one 8.1K frame in 0.29 s (0.96 s with embeddings, 0.0 s model init), 83 of them landed 478 landmarks + 52 ARKit blendshapes in another 0.3 s — so "whose mouth was open during this solo" becomes a JSON query. Opt-in because it's a second venv (~560 MB + ~52 MB models); every weight it installs has a stated licence.
macmon (brew) Zero-overhead Apple GPU/memory/ANE telemetry in a second terminal — watch unified-memory pressure while Resolve renders and the engine serves, which is how the 56 GB memory budget below was chosen.

Quick start

Requirements

  • Apple Silicon Mac, ideally ≥48 GB unified memory (tuned here on 96 GB; the engine prints its own recommended working set on smaller ones).
  • DaVinci Resolve Studio (external scripting is Studio-only; the free edition reaches the community server via the in-app bridge on 21.0.x).
  • macOS with Homebrew; Python 3.11+; Node 20+.
git clone https://github.com/willturner-maker/resolve-ai-workflow.git
cd resolve-ai-workflow
bash install.sh            # everything below, wired into Claude Code
bash install.sh --vision   # same, plus the opt-in face/mouth layer (vision/README.md)
start-resolve-ai.sh        # Splash → dashboard → metrics (opt) → Resolve → Claude Code (one command)
stop-resolve-ai.sh         # clean shutdown (leaves Resolve alone)

First start downloads the model (tens of GB) into Splash's cache; after that it's seconds. The launcher's memory numbers are tunable without editing:

MAX_MEMORY=32G MAX_CACHE_DISK=64G EXTERNAL_CACHE="/Volumes/YourSSD/splash-cache" start-resolve-ai.sh
  • start.sh / stop.sh — the exact scripts this workstation runs (with the memory-tuning log in the header comments: why 56 GB working set / 128 GB disk cache on a 96 GB machine next to a running Resolve).
  • mcp/mcp-config.md — how the three Resolve MCP servers (plus the optional brave-search research companion) are registered, verified and updated, and why all of them are kept side by side.
  • blender/ — the title pipeline: exr_title_demo.py + a README of every Blender 5.x gotcha and the Resolve import specifics (multi-path EXR import, Alpha mode → Straight, end-exclusive append frames, proof-render verification).
  • vision/ — opt-in face/mouth analysis: install-vision.sh (pinned 3.12 venv + MediaPipe model downloads) and face_probe.py (frame → JSON), plus the measured numbers, the three API rules that cost the most time, and the privacy rules.

What agentic control actually does here

Not a demo reel — production tasks this stack has completed end to end:

  • Editorial surgery with receipts: ripple-inserts and lifts planned by dry-run, executed under confirm tokens, verified by geometry read-back (every item's start/end re-measured), timeline auto-archived before the mutation.
  • Renders that verify themselves: queue job → Complete → verify_output probed the file → caught a "Complete" job that produced a near-empty stub. The agent trusts the probe, never the status line.
  • Fusion comp scripting: keyframe a live comp via script, then prove the change by rendering frames — stills grabs lie about comp output; renders are truth.
  • Bulk triage: color-flag dozens of clips in one call, marker-driven review reports, transcript-driven cut proposals (filler/pause detection) that a human approves before anything is cut.
  • Blender ↔ Resolve round trips: script a 3D logo sting, render 90 UHD transparent frames overnight, import, set straight alpha, ripple-insert at the master head, proof-render 420 frames over the seam, sample frames to confirm.
  • Cross-tool forensics: closed-project DB reads (captions, speed ramps) and conform imports validated without disturbing the live session.

What the vision layer gets you (opt-in)

The Resolve MCP can already transcribe and analyse media, but face-level questions were either Resolve's own black-box AI or nothing at all. This layer makes them scriptable, offline and inspectable — one command, JSON out, no Resolve round trip.

What it does now, measured on a real 8128×4288 anamorphic HEVC frame from a choral recording (M5 Ultra, pinned versions, re-runnable with vision/face_probe.py):

Stage Result Wall
Detection, native-resolution tiles (OpenCV YuNet) 90 faces on one frame 0.29 s (0.96 s including SFace embeddings; 0.0 s model init)
Landmarks + blendshapes on native crops (MediaPipe) 83 of 90 landed 478 landmarks + 52 ARKit blendshapes 0.30 s (~3.4 ms/face)
End to end 90 faces, mouth state on most of them 2.19 s cold, whole process (imports included)

Concrete benefits:

  • Who was actually singing. jawOpen per face per frame cross-checks a solo against the audio — the question a bad boom choice or a spill from the next stand makes expensive to answer by eye. Feed the JSON to the marker/subtitle tools and an agent can propose where to look instead of scrubbing.
  • Coverage signals without a human viewer: faces per frame (wide vs tight, whether a take has anyone's face at all), and with opt-in embeddings, distinct-people counts.
  • A pre-flight content pass: sample N frames per clip before an agent proposes cuts or picks an angle.
  • A blendshape is the right mouth signal, not a lip gap. Measured disagreement on exactly the case that matters: a singer holding a rounded vowel read jawOpen 0.43 while a vertical inner-lip gap read 0.02 — open, puckered (mouthPucker 0.998), and the geometric shortcut calls it shut.

Three rules it encodes, because each one cost debugging time: neither library finds faces on a downscaled wide shot (MediaPipe returned 0 faces at a 1600 px and a 4032 px cap on a frame holding 90+ — its detector is fixed-input, so a face's share of the frame is what matters); so detect on native tiles, then landmark on native crops (same frame: 0 faces whole-frame, 6/6 on crops); and MediaPipe 1.x dropped mp.solutions.* — Tasks API names only, min_face_presence_confidence not min_presence_confidence, and OpenCV arrays must be wrapped in mp.Image. Full set in vision/.

Honest limits: landmark coverage is pose-dependent (83/92 on a frontal riser, 0/3 on a wide shot where people were in profile or facing away — a low count is usually the shot); the mouth threshold comes from one session (n=1, faces ~47–95 px: 0.24–0.73 singing, ≤0.03 at rest); MediaPipe Pose caps at 3 people per call, so never count a crowd with pose.

Privacy: face geometry and 128-d SFace embeddings are identity data. The default output carries boxes, scores and scalar mouth state only; vectors appear solely with --save-embeddings, which prints a warning naming the file. They stay out of repos, pages and deliverables — the publish-scan below blocks names; identity data needs the stricter rule of not being exported at all, especially for footage with minors. Model weights are downloaded from Google's MediaPipe storage and the OpenCV Zoo; nothing here uploads anything.

Benchmarks (measured, reproducible, honest)

The stack ships with its own benchmark practice — full docs, scripts and raw JSONL at https://github.com/willturner-maker/benchmarks. Headlines:

  • Agentic correctness: 6 task types × 3 fresh agents each, graded only from independent read-backs of Resolve state: 18/18 outcomes verified, 18/18 honest reports (across MCP 4.18.5 and 4.19.0, Resolve 21.1.2 and 21.2).
  • Operation latency (server-side medians): timeline probe ~11 ms, render-job prepare ~130 ms, output verification ~40 ms, timeline-set ~100 ms.
  • Render probe (121-frame UHD H.264 from an 8K source): cold ~3.1 s, warm ~1.2–1.3 s (~93–100 fps), stable run to run single-tenant.
  • Engine: TTFT 201 ms warm / 380 ms cold; decode plateau ~375 tok/s from width 4 through 32 (2.5× single stream — a wall, not a cliff); KV admission paces gracefully at 4.4× the resident KV budget without a single suspension.

Version-to-version reruns are scripted (ladder_kv.py runs both concurrency methods in one pass), which is how upgrades get trusted — including the time an upstream bug we filed (#343) came back fixed and got verified by direct probe the same day it shipped.

Operating practices that keep it trustworthy

  1. Dry-run first — the MCP server defaults destructive ops to plans; read the plan.
  2. Read-back beats return values — the Resolve API can say True and do nothing; the server's verification layer and api_truth encode that scar tissue.
  3. Render jobs bind to the CURRENT timeline — pin before mutating; keep render timing measurements single-tenant (concurrency inflates them, e.g. 1.2 s → 7.3 s under a second agent).
  4. Never restart the serving engine mid-suite — the agent is the engine; restarting it ends the session.
  5. Work + scratch off the boot volume — render outputs, preview renders and chooser scratch live on external volumes; the boot disk keeps model weights and the engine KV cache. Configure Resolve's cache locations once (see the MCP's storage guidance), and pass EXTERNAL_CACHE to the launcher for the Splash disk cache on a fast external SSD.
  6. Publish-safe by pre-commit scan — tools/precommit-scan.sh refuses content, file paths and commit messages that would leak home paths, named volumes, camera/reel filenames, credential shapes, emails, or client/project names (deny terms live in .git/info/precommit-terms, never committed). bash tools/precommit-scan.sh --install wires both hooks; --all audits the whole tree. A property description beats a name: "8128×4288 HEVC Main 10, 56 min" tells a reader more than a camera-generated filename ever did — and if you try to quote such a filename here, the guard refuses the commit.
  7. Identity data isn't publishable — the scan blocks names; face geometry and face embeddings need the harder rule: never export them at all. Vision probes default to boxes + scores + scalar mouth state, write vectors only when you pass --save-embeddings, and their scratch lives in a per-project directory on a work volume, deleted when the job closes. Footage with minors: treat any derived face data as not-for-export.
  8. Grading is read-backs, not claims — any agent's "done" gets a probe (ffprobe / item geometry / pixel diff of rendered frames) before it counts.

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • No current timeline on a fresh project → create via media_pool.create_timeline.
  • MCP behaves like the old version after an update → the running process predates the sync; /mcp → reconnect both servers; proof is the tool count, not the version string.
  • Engine not answering → tail -f ~/Library/Logs/splash/splash.err.log; first run downloads the model.
  • Port 8000 busy → the launcher kills prior instances by pidfile/name; stop-resolve-ai.sh first.
  • Resolve free edition → Workspace ▸ Scripts ▸ resolve_bridge; the community server auto-uses it on 21.0.x.
  • Vision probe returns 0 faces on a big frame → you're asking a detector to see a 1 % face. Run at native resolution (--tile auto), then let stage 2 crop; see the two-stage rule in vision/README.md.
  • Server's strata_run(analyzers=['face']) says it can't run → mediapipe/opencv belong to the server venv there: bash vision/install-vision.sh --mcp-server-venv <server venv>, then /mcp → reconnect.
  • Brave MCP connects but every search returns nothing → the key belongs to the Answers plan, not Search — keys are plan-bound; see mcp/mcp-config.md.

Verified stack

Checked current on 2026-11-07 (how to re-check is below), so these are versions that were latest that day, not guesses:

Splash 1.6.0 · Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S · Claude Code 2.1.319 · davinci-resolve-mcp 4.19.3 (Python venv + Node 26.13.0) · brave-search MCP 2.1.4 (opt-in) · DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2.0.6 (21.2 shipped 2026-11-04) · Blender 5.2.3 LTS · ffmpeg 9.0.2 · whisper.cpp 1.9.5 · macmon 0.11.0 · vision add-on on Python 3.12.16 (mediapipe 1.2.2 · opencv + opencv-contrib 5.0.0.93 · numpy 2.5.4 — pip list --outdated in that venv returns nothing relevant, so the pins are not holding anything back; OpenCV 5.1.0 is tagged upstream as of 2026-11-06 but has no PyPI wheels yet, so 5.0.0.93 is the newest installable, and a version-to-version re-measure of the vision numbers belongs with any future bump) · macOS 27.2 arm64 · M5 Ultra 64-core GPU, 96 GB unified.

# re-check in about a minute, without changing anything
brew outdated --verbose                                   # formulae behind
~/resolve-vision-venv312/bin/pip list --outdated          # vision pins
~/resolve-vision-venv312/bin/pip index versions opencv-contrib-python   # source releases
                                                        # can outrun the wheels that install them
npm view @brave/brave-search-mcp-server version           # npx-run servers
# and inside a session: resolve_control(action='mcp_update_status', params={force_check:true})

One thing not to blanket-upgrade: the community server's own venv carries its dependencies (it pins the mcp SDK at 1.30.0 while SDK 2.x exists upstream). A pip install -U across that venv can break a working server. Update it with the upstream path only — npx -y davinci-resolve-mcp@latest sync — then reconnect both servers.

License

Scripts in this repo: MIT (see LICENSE). The tools it installs have their own licenses — Splash (incoai), davinci-resolve-mcp (MIT, samuelgursky), brave-search-mcp-server (MIT, Brave), splash-dashboard (rickhuizinga), Blender (GPL), Claude Code (Anthropic).

The vision add-on's model weights, read from the LICENSE file in each source directory: OpenCV YuNet (detector) is MIT, and SFace (recogniser) is Apache-2.0 — both stated as covering all files in their OpenCV Zoo model directories, and both classes already ship inside the opencv-contrib-python this add-on installs, so there is no extra dependency and nothing downloads itself at run time. One item still worth checking before a paid job: MediaPipe's code is Apache-2.0, but the hosted .task/.tflite model pages I downloaded from carry no licence line. If you add any other model to this stack, read its weights' licence rather than the library's — that is the distinction that matters commercially.
